title: Giant magneto-cubic in-plane Hall effect in a nonmagnetic material

paper_content.abstract:
In-plane Hall effect triggered by an external magnetic field applied in the transport plane has
attracted significant experimental attentions in recent few years. However, most experiments focus
on magnetic materials, where the existence of magnetic ordering may complicate understanding
the physics behind, and the relatively small signal magnitudes limit the application of the effect.
Here, we report a giant in-plane Hall effect in a nonmagnetic half-Heusler compound LuAuSn,
with a magnitude exceeding all the previously reported values. A 2𝜋⁄3-period of in-plane Hall
effect and the consistent cubic dependence on the magnetic field are observed, realizing the long-
sought theoretical prediction of magneto-cubic in-plane Hall effect under threefold rotational
symmetry in an unexpected material. The scaling law analysis and first-principles calculations
indicate that extrinsic side jump and skew scattering processes from both impurity and phonon
scatterings dominate the observed effect. These findings unravel a new type of magneto-nonlinear
in-plane Hall effect, and its large magnitude and wide-temperature operation may open the door
to practical applications of in-plane Hall effect.

paper_content.methods:
Single crystal growth. LuAuSn single crystals were grown using the Sn flux method. A
mixture of pure elements with molar ratio Lu: Au: Sn = 1: 1: 10 was placed in an alumina crucible,
which was then sealed in an evacuated quartz ampoule. The quartz ampoule was placed in a pit-
type furnace and heated from room temperature to 1150 ℃, where it was held for 24 hours. It was
then slowly cooled to 650 ℃ at the rate of 2 ℃ per hour for sample #1 and #2. At this point, the
excess Sn flux was removed by centrifugation.

Single crystal characterization. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction and crystal orientation were
done at room temperature using a TD-3500 XRD system and TD-M3000 Laue system, respectively.
The chemical composition of the LuAuSn sample was examined using scanning electron
microscope (SEM) equipped with energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS). EDS measurements were
performed at multiple positions on the crystal surfaces, with results consistent within the
instrumental error margin of 1%−2%.

Physical property characterization. Magneto-transport properties were carried out using a
Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS, 9 T). The angle-dependent electrical transport
measurements were performed using the standard four-probe method with a horizontal rotator. A
universal sample holder board was used for out-of-plane transport measurements, while a parallel
magnetic field sample holder board was used for in-plane transport measurement.

First-principles calculations. First-principles calculations based on density functional
theory were performed using the Vienna ab initio Simulation Package 48-50 with the projector-
augmented wave method 51. The Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof 52 generalized gradient approximation
was employed to treat the exchange-correlation energy. The lattice constant was taken as
6.5627 Å. The inner positions are fully relaxed with force tolerance 0.01 eV Å−1. The Γ-centered
𝑘-point mesh with size 8×8×8 were used for Brillouin zone sampling. The Liechtenstein et
al.'s approach 53 was used to treat localized f orbitals of Lu atoms with an effective 𝑈 = 6.7 eV
and 𝐽 = 0.7 eV 39, 54. The ab initio Wannier tight-binding models were constructed using the
Wannier90 package 55. A dense 𝑘-point mesh with size 300×300×300 were used for Hall
conductivity calculations.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The in-plane Hall effect (IPHE), which was referred to as the "longitudinal Hall effect" in the 1950s, has recently attracted
renewed interest because of its possible connection to band topology. This manuscript reports a systematic study of the
IPHE in the paramagnetic metal LuAuSn, highlighting (i) a B^3-scaling IPHE and (ii) a record-high in-plane Hall conductivity
at 2 K. By comparing the data with first-principles calculations, the authors argue that side-jump and skew-scattering
mechanisms dominate the observed in-plane Hall conductivity. The experimental data are of good quality. However, I am
not convinced that the present findings have sufficient novelty or impact to merit publication in Nature Communications, for
the reasons below.
(i) The authors claim that the paper reports the first experimental observation of a B^3-scaling IPHE in paramagnetic metals.
However, experimental indications of such behavior were already reported as early as the 1950s (Refs. [R1, R2] below). For
instance, in n-type paramagnetic germanium, which shares the same Laue point group (m-3m) as LuAuSn, B^3-scaling and
even B^5-scaling IPHEs were observed [R1]; similarly, a B^3-scaling IPHE was reported in paramagnetic bismuth, albeit not
as the main focus of the study [R2]. Therefore, the authors' claim of "the first observation of magneto-cubic IPHE in a three-
dimensional nonmagnetic material" lacks sufficient justification. I believe the authors should cite these prior works and
clearly describe what is genuinely new in their study.
[R1] L. Grabner, Phys. Rev. 117, 689 (1960).
[R2] T. Okada, J. Phys. Soc. Jpn. 11, 89 (1956); J. Phys. Soc. Jpn. 12, 1327 (1957).
(ii) The manuscript does not sufficiently discuss the physical significance of the B^3-scaling IPHE compared with the more
conventional B-linear IPHE. What new insights—if any—does the analysis of the B^3-scaling IPHE offer that cannot be
obtained from the linear-in-B IPHE? Without such a discussion, the physical significance of the B^3-scaling IPHE remains
unclear.
(iii) I have concerns regarding the symmetry analysis in lines 103–113. First, the statement that there are 14 Laue point
groups is incorrect; the correct number is 11. Moreover, the discussion appears to be formulated in the crystallographic
principal-axis frame. Since tensor components transform under a change of orthonormal basis, a symmetry-forbidden B-
linear IPHE in the principal-axis frame may become allowed in a different coordinate frame. In fact, whether such an IPHE is
symmetry-allowed depends on the choice of the transport plane. Given that the experiments were performed in a tilted frame,
the symmetry argument should be reformulated in a coordinate-independent manner to avoid internal inconsistencies.
(iv) Although the large in-plane Hall conductivity at 2 K is impressive, the conductivity at room temperature is much smaller.
Without a discussion of how in-plane Hall conductivity might be enhanced near room temperature or why the current values
are technologically meaningful, the claim that this work "opens the door to practical applications of IPHE" seems premature.
(v) The scaling law employed in the analysis was originally proposed for the anomalous Hall effect in ferromagnetic metals.
It would be helpful if the authors could clarify why this scaling approach is applicable to the in-plane Hall conductivity in a
paramagnetic metal, especially given its B^3-dependence.
Given the concerns regarding the novelty and impact of the manuscript, I am unable to recommend it for publication in
Nature Communications.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this paper, the authors have demonstrated the in-plane Hall effect in a nonmagnetic half-Heusler compound LuAuSn. The
observed Hall signal with a period of 2pi/3 seems to be large, and the presented analysis using the scaling law may be
helpful for further examining the scattering effects in the in-plane Hall effect. On the other hand, similar observation has been
reported for a nonmagnetic semimetal Cd3As2, which has been publicly available in this past March (arXiv:2503.04195, not
cited) and recently published in Phys. Rev. Lett. Given that the introduction needs to be updated to reflect recent progress on
the “unexpected” nonmagnetic compound, I am currently uncertain about the manuscript’s impact. Further concerns are
outlined below.
1. While it is straightforward from symmetry considerations that the B^3 term contributes to the in-plane Hall effect on the
(111) cubic plane, it is not entirely clear whether the presented data indeed support the proposed interpretation. The curve
shown in Fig. 2g itself appears to be well fitted by the B^3 dependence. On the other hand, a comparable nonlinear behavior
is evident even in the out-of-plane field sweep (theta = 90 deg), as presented in Fig. 2b, where only the field range
dominated by B dependence appears to shift to higher fields. How does the dependence evolve for theta varying from 0 to
90 deg? My concern is that the curve shown in Fig. 2g may be affected by the presence of two types of carriers. In particular,
the density and mobility of holes and electrons are found to be nearly identical (5x10^19 cm-3, 1,700 cm2V-1s-1 and
4x10^19 cm-3, 2,000 cm2V-1s-1), as summarized in Fig. S2, which make it difficult to simply interpret that the in-plane Hall
effect below 3 T is dominated by a single type of carrier.
2. It may be difficult to position LuAuSn this compound as an ideal system of the in-plane Hall effect, and the authors are
encouraged to clarify the limitations more explicitly. As already noted, this compound intrinsically contains two types of
carriers, which is also supported by the band structures in Fig. 5a. This inevitably
complicates the field and temperature dependence of the Hall effect. Furthermore, in
the nonmagnetic cubic system, octupolar as well as linear couplings between the
Hall vector and the magnetic field are allowed, but they are restricted to diagonal ones.
In this situation, the in-plane anomalous Hall effect accidentally appears only when the
measurement plane is not defined by two principal axes, such as the (111) and (103)
planes (see Phys. Rev. X 15, 031006 (2025)., not cited).
3. It is noted that rho_xy of sample #1 in Fig. 2b does not change sign for the
out-of-plane field sweep, whereas sigma_xy in
Fig. 4c changes from negative to positive. Is this from sample #2, or from yet another sample? If so, it would be helpful to
provide basic transport characterization of these samples, as the two-carrier behavior
also differs from sample to sample.
4. Related to the point above, the manuscript would benefit from a more detailed discussion of how off-stoichiometry and
structural disorder in the half-Heusler compound affect presented two-carrier transport and scattering effects, which can differ
from sample to sample. The EDX analysis indicates a slight deviation from the nominal stoichiometric ratio, and the degree
of order/disorder could in principle be quantified from the relative XRD peak intensities. It remains unclear how much
disorder is present in the examined samples including sample #2 or the one displayed in Fig. 4c. Considering that side-jump
and skew-scattering contributions play a large role, it is essential to present whether the first-principles calculations were
carried out for the ordered phase, and how disorder—if included—would alter the theoretical predictions.
5. Considering that multiple fitting parameters are used, how accurately can each contribution be decomposed? How about
the fitting results for sample #2? I also have concerns regarding the direct application of the sigma_xx scaling from single-
carrier systems (Ref. 39) to the multi-carrier system. Does the calculation of the Lorentz-force contributions in Fig. 5c also
take into account multi-carrier effects? The results should be displayed over the same energy range as in Fig. 5b.
6. I am concerned that the main results presented as rho_xy may in fact correspond to rho_yx. In addition, it seems that the
definition of axis handedness is inconsistent between Figs. 2a and 2c, which may result in additional confusion.

in Nature Communications. I recommend acceptance pending minor revisions as outlined above.

effect" in the 1950s, has recently attracted renewed interest because of its possible
connection to band topology. This manuscript reports a systematic study of the IPHE
in the paramagnetic metal LuAuSn, highlighting (i) a B3-scaling IPHE and (ii) a
record-high in-plane Hall conductivity at 2 K. By comparing the data with
first-principles calculations, the authors argue that side-jump and skew-scattering
mechanisms dominate the observed in-plane Hall conductivity. The experimental data

Response to the Report of Reviewer #3
Having thoroughly examined the authors’ detailed point-by-point rebuttal and the
revised manuscript, I am pleased to state that my initial concerns have been
comprehensively and convincingly addressed. The authors have gone to exceptional
lengths to provide not only clear theoretical and experimental clarifications but also
substantial new data that significantly strengthen the manuscript's core claims. The
quality of the response and the depth of the additional analysis are commendable. My
primary reservations regarding the novelty and impact of the work have been fully
resolved. The authors' symmetry-based argument distinguishing their observation in
LuAuSn from earlier reports in materials like germanium is persuasive. They
correctly point out that the experimental configurations in those historical studies
could not isolate a genuine symmetry-protected in-plane Hall effect, making their
work the first clear demonstration of a magneto-cubic IPHE in a well-defined,
three-dimensional nonmagnetic crystalline system. Furthermore, the newly added data
on samples with progressively higher residual resistance ratios (RRR) is a
masterstroke. The clear trend of dramatically enhanced IPHE conductivity with
increasing sample quality provides direct and compelling experimental evidence that
extrinsic scattering mechanisms—namely side-jump and skew-scattering—are
dominant. This successfully shifts the narrative from merely observing a large effect
to understanding its origin and establishing a material-based strategy for its
optimization. The authors have also done an excellent job tackling more technical
concerns. The additional analysis of high-field behavior, including attempts at
higher-order fitting and the discussion of a possible crossover regime, adds valuable
nuance. The demonstration that the scaling law analysis holds for a second sample (#2)
and the clarification of the multi-carrier effects reinforce the robustness of their
conclusions. I appreciate the careful revisions to the symmetry discussion, the updated
comparisons in Figure 4f, and the candid discussion in the manuscript regarding the
inherent limitations of separating individual scattering contributions within the scaling
framework.
In summary, the revised manuscript presents a highly complete and robust study.
It makes a significant contribution by unveiling a new, high-performance material
platform for the in-plane Hall effect, firmly establishing the role of extrinsic
mechanisms in generating a record-large response, and providing a clear path for
future material engineering. The work undoubtedly meets the high standards for
publication in Nature Communications.
For final polishing, I only suggest a few minor editorial points. (1) Please ensure
a brief note is added to the figure captions or methods to clarify which specific sample
(#1, #2, etc.) corresponds to each main figure panel, as this was discussed in the
rebuttal. (2) The phrasing on the high-field behavior in the discussion could be
slightly refined to more explicitly frame the deviation from B³ scaling as an entry
point into the interesting physics of non-perturbative magnetic field regimes. (3)
Finally, a final check to ensure all key data from the rebuttal (like the RRR vs.
conductivity table and the temperature-field phase diagram) are seamlessly integrated
into the main text or supplementary information would be beneficial.
I am fully satisfied with the authors' responses and the state of the manuscript. I
recommend acceptance in its current form.

dimensional nonmagnetic material" lacks sufficient justification. I believe the authors should cite these prior works and
clearly describe what is genuinely new in their study.
[R1] L. Grabner, Phys. Rev. 117, 689 (1960).
[R2] T. Okada, J. Phys. Soc. Jpn. 11, 89 (1956); J. Phys. Soc. Jpn. 12, 1327 (1957).

symmetry-allowed depends on the choice of the transport plane. Given that the experiments were performed in a tilted frame,

are technologically meaningful, the claim that this work "opens the door to practical applications of IPHE" seems premature.

It would be helpful if the authors could clarify why this scaling approach is applicable to the in-plane Hall conductivity in a
paramagnetic metal, especially given its B^3-dependence.
Given the concerns regarding the novelty and impact of the manuscript, I am unable to recommend it for publication in
Nature Communications.

In this paper, the authors have demonstrated the in-plane Hall effect in a nonmagnetic half-Heusler compound LuAuSn. The

outlined below.
1. While it is straightforward from symmetry considerations that the B^3 term contributes to the in-plane Hall effect on the
(111) cubic plane, it is not entirely clear whether the presented data indeed support the proposed interpretation. The curve
shown in Fig. 2g itself appears to be well fitted by the B^3 dependence. On the other hand, a comparable nonlinear behavior
is evident even in the out-of-plane field sweep (theta = 90 deg), as presented in Fig. 2b, where only the field range

90 deg? My concern is that the curve shown in Fig. 2g may be affected by the presence of two types of carriers. In particular,

4x10^19 cm-3, 2,000 cm2V-1s-1), as summarized in Fig. S2, which make it difficult to simply interpret that the in-plane Hall

encouraged to clarify the limitations more explicitly. As already noted, this compound intrinsically contains two types of
carriers, which is also supported by the band structures in Fig. 5a. This inevitably
complicates the field and temperature dependence of the Hall effect. Furthermore, in

measurement plane is not defined by two principal axes, such as the (111) and (103)

structural disorder in the half-Heusler compound affect presented two-carrier transport and scattering effects, which can differ

## Abstract

In-plane Hall effect triggered by an external magnetic field applied in the transport plane has

## Methods

Single crystal growth. LuAuSn single crystals were grown using the Sn flux method. A
mixture of pure elements with molar ratio Lu: Au: Sn = 1: 1: 10 was placed in an alumina crucible,
which was then sealed in an evacuated quartz ampoule. The quartz ampoule was placed in a pit-
type furnace and heated from room temperature to 1150 ℃, where it was held for 24 hours. It was
then slowly cooled to 650 ℃ at the rate of 2 ℃ per hour for sample #1 and #2. At this point, the
excess Sn flux was removed by centrifugation.

Single crystal characterization. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction and crystal orientation were
done at room temperature using a TD-3500 XRD system and TD-M3000 Laue system, respectively.
The chemical composition of the LuAuSn sample was examined using scanning electron
microscope (SEM) equipped with energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS). EDS measurements were
performed at multiple positions on the crystal surfaces, with results consistent within the
instrumental error margin of 1%−2%.

Physical property characterization. Magneto-transport properties were carried out using a
Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS, 9 T). The angle-dependent electrical transport
measurements were performed using the standard four-probe method with a horizontal rotator. A
universal sample holder board was used for out-of-plane transport measurements, while a parallel
magnetic field sample holder board was used for in-plane transport measurement.

First-principles calculations. First-principles calculations based on density functional
theory were performed using the Vienna ab initio Simulation Package 48-50 with the projector-
augmented wave method 51. The Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof 52 generalized gradient approximation
was employed to treat the exchange-correlation energy. The lattice constant was taken as
6.5627 Å. The inner positions are fully relaxed with force tolerance 0.01 eV Å−1. The Γ-centered

and 𝐽 = 0.7 eV 39, 54. The ab initio Wannier tight-binding models were constructed using the
Wannier90 package 55. A dense 𝑘-point mesh with size 300×300×300 were used for Hall
conductivity calculations.
